national_articles.headline: SEBI raises ISIN maturity cap to 17 per financial year for privately placed debt securities
national_articles.body: Markets regulator Sebi has relaxed norms for debt securities issued on a private placement basis, allowing an issuer to have up to 17 International Securities Identification Numbers (ISINs) maturing in a single financial year. An International Securities Identification Number (ISIN) is a unique 12-character alphanumeric code used globally to identify specific securities, such as bonds, stocks, derivatives, and mutual funds. Under the revised norms, six ISINs will be available for the issuance of the capital gains tax debt securities by the authorised issuers under section 54EC of the Income Tax Act, 1961 on a private placement basis,Sebisaid in a circular on Wednesday. Of the 17 ISINs, a maximum of 12 ISINs can mature in a financial year for plain vanilla debt securities, covering both secured and unsecured instruments, it added. Sebi said that if the total outstanding amount across these 12 ISINs maturing in a financial year reaches Rs 15,000 crore, then one additional ISIN may be permitted for every additional issuance of Rs 3,000 crore. A maximum of five ISINs maturing in a financial year, will be allowed for structured debt securities, market-linked debt securities, floating rate bonds, zero coupon bonds and debt capital instruments (Tier II bonds). Existing ISINs pertaining to these bonds will be grandfathered to avoid any unintended breach of ISIN cap, Sebi said. The regulator further excluded Government of India serviced/extra budgetary resources bonds and environment, social and governance debt securities while calculating the applicable ISIN limits for an issuer.  The provisions of this circular will come into force with immediate effect, the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) said.

national_articles.headline: Loans to get costlier as PNB, Indian Bank, Bank of Baroda, others raise rates after RBI repo rate hike
national_articles.body: Market Mastery Find the weak links Hours after RBI raised its benchmark policy rate, large banks such as Punjab National Bank, Indian Bank and Bank of Baroda announced an increase in their lending rates, making loans expensive for borrowers. The Reserve Bank of India raised its benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 per cent on Wednesday, its first increase in nearly four years, and signalled that further hikes could follow as rising inflation and a weakening currency prompt a policy pivot. The six-member Monetary Policy Committee voted unanimously to raise the repo rate, the first such increase since Governor Sanjay Malhotra took office in December 2024. While the move was widely expected, the central bank sprang a surprise in shifting its stance towards "calibrated tightening", effectively ruling out a rate cut in the near term. Punjab National Bank (PNB), in a regulatory filing, said that consequent upon an increase in the repo rate by the RBI, the bank has revised Repo Linked Lending Rate (RLLR) from 8.10 per cent (including BSP of 0.35 per cent) to 8.35 per cent (including BSP of 0.35 per cent) with effect from October 8. However, the country's second-largest public sector lender said the Marginal Cost of Lending Rate (MCLR) and Base Rate would remain unchanged. Chennai-based public sector lender Indian Bank also increased its Repo Linked Benchmark Lending Rates (RBLR) to 8.20 per cent against the existing 7.95 per cent. In line with the increase in the policy repo rate of 25 basis points by RBI's Monetary Policy Committee (MPC), the revised rate of the bank would be effective from October 8, Indian Bank said in a separate filing. Another large public sector lender, Bank of Baroda (BoB), increased its Repo Based Lending Rate to 8.15 per cent from the existing 7.90 per cent, an increase of 25 basis points. Bank of India (BoI) and Indian Overseas Bank (IOB) also raised its Repo Based Lending Rate (RBLR) to 8.35 per cent effective October 8. The revision follows the RBI's upward revision of the repo rate, BoI said in a regulatory filing. On the private sector side, Tamilnad Mercantile Bank increased its Repo Linked Lending Rate (RLLR) to 8.5 per cent from the existing 8.25 per cent.  Other lenders are expected to announce an increase in their benchmark lending rate in line with RBI's decision.

national_articles.headline: Private banks' share in tri-party repo borrowing falls sharply in H1FY27: RBI report
national_articles.body: Private sector banks' share in borrowing through the tri-party repo market declined sharply to 14 per cent in the first half of 2026-27 compared to 24 per cent in the preceding six-month period, according to the RBI's monetary policy report released on Wednesday. Tri-party repo (repurchase) borrowing involves a third-party agency to manage collateral assets to facilitate aloantransaction between a lender and borrower. State-owned banks increased their share in the collateralised overnight money market to 35 per cent during April-September 2026 from 32 per cent in the preceding half-year period, indicating a shift in the composition of lenders. The shift comes as collateralised segments, comprising tri-party repo and market repo, continued to dominate the overnight money market, accounting for 97 per cent of the total volume during the first half of 2026-27. The uncollateralised call money market accounted for the remaining 3 per cent, with its share remaining broadly unchanged during the period. On the lending side, mutual funds continued to be the largest lenders in the tri-party repo market, with their share remaining unchanged at 65 per cent during the first half of the fiscal. However, their share in total lending in the market repo segment declined to 41 per cent in the first half of 2026-27 from 48 per cent in the preceding half-year period. At the same time, foreign banks increased their share in market repo lending to 31 per cent during the first half from 29 per cent in the preceding six months.  The share of public sector banks in market repo borrowing also increased by 5 percentage points to 13 per cent during the first half of 2026-27.

national_articles.headline: RBI to conduct 29-day VRRR auction for Rs 2 lakh crore on October 8
national_articles.body: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) will conduct a 29-day Variable Rate Reverse Repo (VRRR) auction for Rs 2 lakh crore on October 8 as it continues to manage surplus liquidity in the banking system. Earlier in the day, the RBI absorbed Rs 2.56 lakh crore through an overnight VRRR auction, against the notified amount of Rs 3 lakh crore, at a cut-off rate of 5.49%. RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra, during the Monetary Policy Committee meeting review, said the current liquidity surplus was unlikely to persist for long and that the central bank would use an appropriate mix of tools to manage liquidity. “There is surplus liquidity, but we believe that this is not a very long term phenomenon,” Malhotra said at the post-policy press conference. A money market trader at a state-owned bank said liquidity would gradually drain from the banking system through forex operations and currency in circulation. “There will be a systematic leakage of liquidity from the banking system through forex operations and currency in circulation. The festive season is likely to increase cash demand, while the harvesting and subsequent sowing cycles could also lead to some liquidity outflow. “These factors could absorb around Rs 2-3 lakh crore in the near term, up to January. The RBI’s forward book of more than $100 billion could further absorb liquidity as these forwards are delivered. Against this backdrop, the 29-day VRRR is a temporary measure to manage surplus liquidity,” he added. The RBI has been using VRRR auctions to absorb excess funds while allowing liquidity conditions to adjust as these factors play out. It had also conducted a 29-day VRRR auction in September, making the latest operation a similar-duration tool to manage the surplus over the near term. System liquidity has remained in substantial surplus in recent months, largely following capital inflows through measures such as FCNR(B) deposits and dollar-rupee swap operations. According to the RBI’s latest data, the banking system had a surplus of Rs 4.93 lakh crore on Tuesday. The surplus had crossed Rs 11 lakh crore in early September, prompting the RBI to use VRRR auctions and open market operation (OMO) bond sales to absorb excess liquidity. Quarterly advance-tax outflows subsequently moderated the surplus. Malhotra said natural factors would gradually absorb part of the excess liquidity, including currency leakage and banks’ reserve requirements.  “Within this financial year itself, I expect a large amount of this liquidity without giving numbers. 3-4 lakh crore rupees is generally the CIC leakage that happens,” he said, referring to currency in circulation.

international_articles.headline: France bans stun grenade after teen’s hand is amputated: What is EF-SON and how dangerous is it?
international_articles.body: Market Mastery Find the weak links France has suspended the use of a new-generation stun grenade after a 15-year-old student suffered severe injuries to his hand during clashes linked to high school protests in the northern city of Lens. The provisional suspension of the EF-SON grenade was ordered by French national police director general Louis Laugier. He said the measure would remain in force “until the circumstances of the young man's injury in Lens are established.” Interior Minister Laurent Nunez also confirmed the suspension during an interview with RTL, saying: “I am suspending its use for the high school student protests until all the facts are known regarding what happened in this case.” Nuñez said France's police oversight body, IGPN, has opened 18 investigations into allegations of police violence during the protests. What happened in Lens? The incident involving the 15-year-old has become a major point of contention amid escalating student protests across France. The teenager's mother told BFMTV that her son's hand had to be amputated. “His life has been stolen. He’s a 15-year-old kid; how can children be treated like that?,” she said, adding that her son did not pick up the grenade. There are conflicting accounts of what happened immediately before the grenade exploded. AFP, citing a police union source, reported that the teenager appeared to have picked up a sting-ball grenade used by riot police, which subsequently exploded in his hand. However, La Voix du Nord quoted a girl who said she was standing close to the teenager when the incident occurred. She disputed that account. “He didn't pick it up. I was there; I saw it. He didn't pick it up; he didn't catch it,” she was quoted as saying. Lens Mayor Sylvain Robert said the circumstances surrounding the incident had yet to be established. “Like you, and like many others, I have seen some videos showing the aftermath. But I did not see how the operation was organised, either by the police or by the students,” Robert told a French publication, according to the BBC. Why France suspended the grenade The weapon at the centre of the controversy is the EF-SON, manufactured by French company Alsetex, which has a long-standing commercial relationship with the Interior Ministry. French law enforcement agencies began using the EF-SON in 2025, alongside another stun grenade, the GL-304, manufactured by Brazil's Condor. The EF-SON is designed to be fired from a 40-millimetre grenade launcher. It is not compatible with the Cougar launcher traditionally used by French police, but can be fired from the Cobra launcher, a dual-barrel system introduced into French police use in 2025. The national police has now suspended its use in high school protests while the circumstances of the Lens incident are investigated. Protests spread across France The grenade controversy comes as France faces sustained protests involving thousands of students and other demonstrators. More than 500 schools were fully or partially closed on October 7, according to Education Minister Édouard Geffray. Speaking in the National Assembly, Geffray said 24 schools had been “vandalised” to such an extent that they had remained closed for weeks. High school students have blockaded schools in several cities, including Marseille and Strasbourg. Demonstrators have carried flags, placards and smoke flares. In Paris, protesters displayed a slogan reading “under our textbooks, anger”, a reference to the famous “under the paving stones, the beach” slogan associated with the May 1968 student protests. The protests have also triggered allegations of disproportionate police force, with rights groups and protesters demanding greater scrutiny of law enforcement actions. What is driving the student protests? The demonstrations have been fuelled by complaints about conditions in France's public education system. Students and teachers have raised concerns about overcrowded classrooms, unfilled teaching positions and ageing school infrastructure. Class sizes in some schools are reported to exceed 34 to 38 students, making individual attention more difficult and putting additional pressure on classroom capacity. The shortage of teachers has also affected students' access to regular lessons. Reports have highlighted gaps in subjects including mathematics, physics and modern languages, with schools struggling to find replacement teachers. School buildings have emerged as another major concern. High temperatures have exposed problems involving ageing infrastructure, poor insulation and inadequate ventilation and climate-control systems in some French schools. Macron faces pressure over unrest President Emmanuel Macron has faced criticism over his response as the protests have intensified. During a state visit to Madrid last week, Macron acknowledged the concerns among young people while condemning violence. “I understand the anxieties and anger that our youth might feel, whether that’s related to the climate, new technologies, or geopolitical tensions. However, none of these fears justifies violence,” Macron said. On Tuesday night, Macron summoned senior officials, including Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez and Education Minister Édouard Geffray, for discussions on the unrest. Macron was also seen testing a new ballistic missile designed for France's future defence needs while the protests were continuing. The development prompted criticism on social media, including from X user Collin Rugg, who wrote: “French President Emmanuel Macron shows off France’s new ballistic missile to “protect the French in the long term against threats”. The test comes as riots are breaking out throughout France. I hate to break this to you, but the threats are already in your country.” The government has continued to distinguish between the grievances driving the protests and acts of violence or vandalism.  For now, the suspension of the EF-SON grenade remains provisional, with French authorities awaiting the findings of investigations into the Lens incident and wider allegations of police misconduct.

international_articles.headline: Oil shipping costs reach dizzying new highs on Hormuz snarls
international_articles.body: The price of hiring supertankers to transport oil surged to a fresh high, adding huge costs to the petroleum supply chain. It now costs $77 million to hire a very large crude carrier to move US oil to Asia, according to data from the Baltic Exchange in London on Wednesday. The average in 2025 was $9.2 million. While headline oil futures are trading at around the $100-a-barrel mark, those futures are typically based on grades at the point of export. For a 2 million barrel cargo, the freight price implies an additional delivery cost of about $38.50 a barrel. In some markets, like West Africa, sellers are being forced to discount their cargoes at the point of export.  The Iran war has brought chaos to the tanker market, redrawing how oil leaves the Middle East and adding huge amounts of time to the process. While the region’s flows have been rebounding in recent weeks, the trade is far more complicated than it was before the Iran war, adding to delivery times and effectively slashing fleet supply.

international_articles.headline: America wants an AI boom, China wants ‘human control’, Europe wants tough rules: How the 3 powers are regulating AI
international_articles.body: Market Mastery Find the weak links The United States, China and the European Union are taking different paths to govern artificial intelligence, as calls grow worldwide to rein in its most powerful systems. Here is how they are going about it: United States Nearly two years into his second term, PresidentDonald Trumphas built his AI policy almost entirely from voluntary industry pledges and executive orders intended to sustain an AI boom that is powering the US economy. On his first day back in office, Trump scrapped his predecessor Joe Biden's 2023 order requiring developers of the most powerful AI systems to share safety test results with the government. In July 2025, the White House unveiled an "AI Action Plan" listing more than 90 measures to speed up development. An accompanying order titled "Preventing Woke AI in the Federal Government" requires federal agencies to buy only models deemed ideologically neutral. Congress, politically divided and heavily lobbied by Big Tech, has yet to pass a federal AI law, and is out of session until after the midterm elections. Trump has pushed to block state AI laws, but Congress has repeatedly refused to override them, and state laws are taking effect nationwide. This year, the release of AI models capable of powerful cyberattacks shifted the focus to security. A June order set up a voluntary system for developers to give the government up to 30 days of early access to their most powerful models. With voter anxiety growing, the heads of major AI companies signed a White House accord on September 29 pledging independent audits and board-level oversight of cutting-edge models. The pact carries no penalties for companies that fall short, though Trump called it "morally binding." The same day, Trump ordered federal agencies to replace the term "artificial intelligence" with "super intelligence" in official communications. China China already has a complex, evolving set of rules on how AI is used, including by children. Regulations on AI companion bots took effect in July, aiming to curb emotional dependency and banning the creation of digital clones of real people without their consent. President Xi Jinping said this summer that AI should be "always under human control," calling for more "laws and regulations, technological monitoring, early warning, and emergency response systems." Premier Li Qiang has also warned that the world risks "losing control" of frontier technologies such as AI if governments are too slow to regulate them. However, "a general pause or deliberate slowdown in AI development remains outside the mainstream Chinese policy posture," Oxford China Policy Lab analysts wrote in September. Some in China see calls to slow progress as hard to justify, "particularly given their perception that US measures such as export controls have already constrained China's AI development for years," they said. China censors and controls AI-generated content much as it does other online information -- and last month, its spy chief warned that AI could endanger national security. "Hostile forces" are abusing generative AI to "fabricate political rumors and spread harmful information," Minister of State Security Chen Yixin said. Europe The European Union rushed to adopt its AI Act in 2024, which Brussels touts as the world's most comprehensive rules on the technology. But European companies, fearing the rules would stifle innovation as they race to catch up with US and Chinese rivals, later won a delay on rules covering high-risk systems. Amid growing global calls for control, European Commission chief Ursula von der Leyen said last month that the AI rules put "Europe in the position to shape global efforts." She also said she would invite the main frontier labs "for a discussion on how we can support ongoing industry efforts to pace the frontier." European firms have been more wary of slowing down, fearing it could be an attempt by US giants to lock in their dominance. The EU has other tools to regulate AI. In August, ChatGPT became the first AI chatbot added to the EU's list of digital services subject to greater legal scrutiny under its online content rules. Brussels last month also proposed forcing companies to make AI companions and chatbots safe before children use them.  AI chatbots must not "simulate interpersonal relationships in ways that create emotional dependency," the EU said, following a spate of suicides worldwide linked to children's interactions with such assistants.

international_articles.headline: Trump wants to turn his Florida golf course into a new Camp David for future US presidents: What’s behind the plan
international_articles.body: Market Mastery Find the weak links Donald Trump wants to turn his luxury Florida golf course into retreat for future US presidents modeled on the historic Camp David getaway, the White House said Wednesday. The plan would make the Trump International Club in West Palm Beach -- where the 80-year-old billionaire often spends weekends on the fairway -- into an official sanctuary for his successors. "The United States government has asked to look into developing a Presidential retreat at Trump International Golf Course in Palm Beach for future presidents, so they can hold important meetings and utilize the amenities of a world-class property," a White House official told AFP on condition of anonymity. The official stressed the security at Trump's course, where gunman Ryan Routh was convicted of trying to assassinate the then-presidential candidate in September 2024. "The property is minutes away from the Donald J. Trump International Airport, does not have buildings looming, does not have houses along the course, has great security features, is close to law enforcement, and happens to be a highly-rated golf course. "These are features that are necessary for any Presidential retreat." Palm Beach international airport was renamed after the city's most famous resident earlier this year. A lawyer representing the Trump course wrote to local officials in September comparing the proposed retreat to Camp David, Windsor Castle in Britain and France's Elysee Palace, the Washington Post reported. Trump is not a fan of Camp David, having visited the presidential bolthole in the scenic Maryland hills near Washington on only a handful of occasions during his two terms in office.  Where other presidents have made frequent journeys and hosted historic foreign summits there, Trump prefers to spend his downtime at his golf courses in Florida and New Jersey.
